reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: An abnormal communication between a coronary artery and a cardiac chamber or great vessel, bypassing the myocardial capillary bed
Most drain into low-pressure right-sided structures such as the right ventricle, right atrium, coronary sinus or pulmonary artery
A continuous murmur is characteristic and is often louder in diastole, differing from the classic ductus murmur in location
Coronary steal can divert flow away from the myocardium distal to the fistula, causing ischaemia despite normal epicardial arteries
Many small fistulae are asymptomatic and found incidentally, whereas large ones cause a significant left-to-right shunt and volume loading
Complications include heart failure, arrhythmia, aneurysmal dilatation of the feeding artery, thrombosis and rarely rupture
Closure by transcatheter device or coil, or surgical ligation, is considered for large or symptomatic fistulae
reference.pathophysiology: A coronary artery fistula is a direct channel connecting a coronary artery to a cardiac chamber or great vessel, so blood bypasses the intramyocardial capillary network. Because the drainage site is usually a lower-pressure right-sided structure, flow runs continuously throughout the cardiac cycle, producing a continuous murmur and a left-to-right shunt when drainage is into the venous circulation. The chronically high flow dilates and can aneurysmally enlarge the feeding artery. Flow preferentially runs down the low-resistance fistulous track rather than into the higher-resistance distal myocardial bed, a coronary steal that may cause regional ischaemia. Large shunts impose volume loading on the receiving chambers and can lead to heart failure and pulmonary overcirculation over time.
additionalDifferentials: Anomalous origin of a coronary artery from the pulmonary artery
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography with colour Doppler to localise the fistula and its drainage site
Coronary CT angiography to define the course and drainage of the fistula
Cardiac catheterisation with coronary angiography as the reference standard and for shunt quantification
Cardiac MRI to assess chamber volumes and shunt magnitude
Electrocardiogram and exercise testing for evidence of ischaemia
Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora in large shunts
redFlags: Anginal symptoms or evidence of myocardial ischaemia from coronary steal
Heart failure from a large left-to-right shunt
A rapidly enlarging or aneurysmal feeding coronary artery
Arrhythmia, thrombosis or signs of impending rupture
reference.prognosis: Small fistulae often remain benign and may close spontaneously, while large or symptomatic fistulae carry risks of ischaemia, heart failure and aneurysm; outcomes after device or surgical closure are generally favourable.
pitfalls: Attributing a continuous murmur to a ductus and missing the fistula on the coronary vessels
Assuming normal epicardial coronaries exclude ischaemia despite ongoing steal
Underestimating the shunt in a large fistula draining to the right heart
Overlooking aneurysmal dilatation of the feeding artery and its thrombotic risk
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Observe small asymptomatic fistulae with periodic imaging, as many remain benign and some close spontaneously
Close large or symptomatic fistulae definitively by transcatheter device occlusion or surgical ligation
Use antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy where the feeding artery is aneurysmally dilated or thrombotic risk is high, and following closure
Treat volume-loading heart failure with diuretics and address ischaemia arising from coronary steal
Monitor with echocardiography, cross-sectional imaging and, where needed, angiography for shunt size, aneurysm and post-closure patency
Refer to a congenital cardiology service for intervention planning
Escalate for heart failure, arrhythmia, aneurysmal enlargement or thrombotic complications
